newsitem.title: UK: Iraqi crude seen displacing Russian Urals in Med.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi crude seen displacing Russian Urals in Med.

text.p: Iraqi crude oil will not be able to travel far beyond Europe and the Mediterranean if exports resume soon given market economics and an unworkable transatlantic route, traders said.
With an API of 36 for Kirkuk export grade, Iraqi oil is expected to displace similar quality Russian Urals at current prices in these markets, they added.

Urals, the Mediterranean sour benchmark, has been trading at higher numbers recently because of tight supplies caused partly by weather delays at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiisk and pipeline maintenance.
Urals traded on Monday at Dated Brent -38 cents, up some 20 cents on previous deals.

Russian crude sales into the region benefited from Iraq's six-year absence but the prospect of resumed Iraqi exports, which now seem possible in the first quarter of 1997, will give Urals a run for its money.

Under the pricing formula submitted by Iraq to the United Nations for implementing the oil-for-food deal, Kirkuk crude exports from Turkey's Ceyhan terminal will sell at a discount of $1.3-$1.5 a barrel to Dated Brent.
Physical Brent, the world benchmark for Westbound crude, was valued at $22.68 a barrel on Tuesday.
Iraq's Basrah Light crude, exported from the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr, will be priced at the Oman/Dubai average.
At current prices, Iraq is likely to export somewhere between 500,000 and 700,000 bpd of sour crude.
Iranian Light, which is of similar quality to Iraqi oil, will also have to compete with Kirkuk oil in the Med, traders said.

"Urals in the Mediterranean and some sales of Iranian Light out of Sidi Kreir will suffer but globally if you look at the flat price movement, Iraq's return will not be a big factor," an oil industry source said.
"The pricing looks very attractive relative to Urals," he added.

At present, it is expensive to move Middle Eastern and West African crude priced against Brent to the U.S. or South American markets because North Sea Brent is too expensive compared with U.S. light crude WTI.
Before 1990, when Iraq invaded Kuwait and invited U.N. sanctions against it, Iraq exported 3.14 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude.
The North American market absorbed 33 percent of Iraqi exports in the eight months to August 1990, according to OPEC figures.

"The way Brent/WTI is now, if you bring any cargo now, it has to stay in Europe. At the inception of this oil, it is more likely to stay in Europe, especially if it comes in January when supplies of Urals is low. That would be ideal timing," an oil company trader said.
Another oil industry source said once Russian domestic consumption eases during the second quarter of 1997, sour differentials in the Med could slump.
Although U.S. companies will not be barred from lifting Iraqi crude, traders say they are unlikely to lift large volumes. Brazil too was among Iraq's biggest customers.
"The market has changed very much since Iraq last exported oil," said an oil trader in Italy.

OPEC powerhouse Saudi Arabia, which virtually alone made up for the shortfall of Iraqi crude by raising its output to 8.0 million bpd, will not suffer any loss of market share and neither would Kuwait, traders said.
Under the partial oil sales deal, Iraq should sell oil at "fair market prices", which prevent it undercutting other producers.
Traders expected some Iraqi crude to find its way to the spot market if no term contracts are available.
Iraq has met with some of its pre-Gulf War customers and state marketing company SOMO has assured buyers its crude will have the same specifications as before.
SOMO has already had meetings in Baghdad with representatives from some oil companies, such as France's Total SA. France was one of Iraq's strongest supporters during the prolonged U.N. negotiations.
-- Kate Dourian, London newsroom +44 171 542 4088
